articles.title: Alpha-Methylacyl-CoA Racemase (AMACR) Deficiency Presenting with Epilepsy, Cognitive Decline, and Pigmentary Retinopathy.
articles.abstract: A 66-year-old woman with long-standing epilepsy and progressive cognitive decline presented with bilateral vision loss (best-corrected visual acuity 1.22 logMAR right eye, 1.10 logMAR left eye). Electrodiagnostic testing showed severe rod-cone dysfunction. Fundus autofluorescence revealed bilateral multifocal geographic hypoautofluorescent lesions with hyperautofluorescent borders in a wreath-like pericentral distribution. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated bilateral outer retinal atrophy with ellipsoid zone loss and cystoid macular edema in the left eye. Genetic testing identified a pathogenic AMACR variant (c.154T>C; p.Ser52Pro) and a variant of uncertain significance (c.704C>T; p.Ala235Val). Elevated pristanic acid (152.9 μmol/L) confirmed alpha-methylacyl-CoA racemase (AMACR) deficiency, explaining her neurological disease. Macular edema decreased by 50 μm with topical dorzolamide and a phytanic and pristanic acid-restricted diet, and she reported subjective neurological improvement. Retinal imaging may be the first diagnostic clue to this rare but treatable condition. Ophthalmologists should consider AMACR deficiency in unexplained pigmentary retinopathy with neurological disease.

articles.title: Feasibility and Early Outcomes of Gonioscopy-Assisted Transluminal Trabeculotomy for Neovascular Glaucoma.
articles.abstract: This retrospective observational case series evaluates the clinical outcomes of gonioscopy-assisted transluminal trabeculotomy (GATT) in 6 consecutive eyes with neovascular glaucoma (NVG) treated at a tertiary referral center. NVG was defined as secondary glaucoma associated with retinal ischemia, characterized by elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) and prior presence of iris and/or angle neovascularization. All patients had previously undergone pan-retinal photocoagulation and intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor therapy and were receiving maximally tolerated medical treatment at presentation. Circumferential GATT was successfully completed in all cases. At final follow-up, IOP control was achieved in 3 eyes with topical therapy, while the remaining 3 eyes required subsequent Ahmed glaucoma valve implantation due to early surgical failure. All eyes that met failure criteria demonstrated circumferential peripheral anterior synechiae formation during early postoperative follow-up and were observed in patients with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus. Two cases required anterior chamber washout for persistent hyphema. In this small case series, our observations suggest that clinical role of GATT remains uncertain and the present data do not allow identification of patient subgroups that may benefit or support definition of clinical indications.

articles.title: Fatty Acids for the Treatment of Ocular Diseases and Ocular Drug Delivery.
articles.abstract: The intricate anatomical and physiological barriers of the eye severely limit the bioavailability of conventional topical therapies, necessitating innovative strategies. In this review, fatty acids are presented as versatile agents functioning in two distinct roles. As bioactive lipids, specific fatty acids exert disease-modifying effects, offering novel pharmacological interventions for ocular surface and posterior segment disorders, including dry eye syndrome, uveitis, and retinal degeneration. Concurrently, beyond their biological activity, fatty acids serve as structural components in formulation design; their physicochemical properties, particularly varying chain lengths and degrees of unsaturation, enable the construction of advanced ocular drug delivery systems with substantially enhanced ocular bioavailability. Crucially, this review not only summarizes the translational prospects of fatty acid-based therapeutics but also highlights the structure-activity relationships governing the in vivo performance of fatty acid-integrated delivery systems. By delineating these dual functionalities, we provide a clear framework for distinguishing nutritional or pharmacological supplementation from excipient or carrier design, thereby facilitating the rational development of next-generation ophthalmic formulations.

articles.title: A clinical multimodal vision language foundation model with fine-grain explainability.
articles.abstract: Despite their considerable promise, many current medical foundation models remain modality specific and lack transparent reasoning, limiting clinical adoption. To address this gap, we introduce Explainable Vision Language Foundation Model for Medicine (EVLF-FM), a multimodal vision language foundation model that combines broad diagnostic capabilities with fine-grained explainability. The development and testing of EVLF-FM encompassed more than 1.3 million total samples from 18 global datasets across 10 imaging modalities related to six clinical specialties: dermatology, hepatology, ophthalmology, pathology, pulmonology and radiology. External validation employed 13,443 independent test samples from 17 additional datasets across 10 imaging modalities. EVLF-FM supports disease diagnosis, visual question answering and pixel-level visual grounding with reasoning capabilities. In internal validation for disease diagnostics, EVLF-FM achieved the highest average accuracy, 0.895, outperforming leading generalist and specialist models. In medical visual grounding, EVLF-FM also achieved reasonable performance across nine modalities with average accuracy at 0.5 intersection over union (Acc@0.5) of 0.842. External testing further confirmed consistent zero-shot and few-shot performance, with competitive F1 scores despite a smaller model size. A hybrid training strategy combining supervised and visual reinforcement fine-tuning enables EVLF-FM to generate clinically interpretable explanations aligned with visual evidence. Human evaluation of these reasoning outputs using the S.C.O.R.E. framework yielded a high overall mean score of 4.25/5, supporting their clinical interpretability. Current limitations include the need for additional validation across diverse healthcare settings. Prospective clinical studies are required to evaluate the safety, effectiveness and clinical utility of EVLF-FM before routine clinical deployment.

articles.title: Red and near-infrared photobiomodulation in precision medicine: mechanisms, dosimetry, and clinical translation.
articles.abstract: Phototherapy is a non-invasive therapeutic modality that uses specific wavelengths of light to modulate biological processes and treat disease. Driven by advances in photobiology, regenerative medicine, and clinical technology, phototherapy has evolved from empirical heliotherapy into a mechanism-based intervention with expanding medical applications. This review places the biological effects, therapeutic indications, and safety profiles of ultraviolet, blue, and green light in comparative context, while focusing primarily on the mechanisms, dosimetry, and clinical translation of red and near-infrared photobiomodulation (PBM). Although ultraviolet and blue light therapies have established roles in dermatology and neonatal jaundice, their clinical use is limited by concerns such as photocarcinogenesis, retinal phototoxicity, and circadian disruption. In contrast, red and near-infrared light offer deeper tissue penetration and, when appropriately dosed, a comparatively low risk of direct photochemical injury. Through mitochondrial, redox, inflammatory, and other context-dependent signaling pathways, red/NIR PBM has been investigated in wound repair, chronic pain, osteoarthritis, musculoskeletal disorders, neurological conditions, and dermatological applications. As a representative quantitative example, a 2024 meta-analysis of 10 placebo-controlled randomized trials involving 542 participants with knee osteoarthritis found a moderate reduction in pain at rest with PBM compared with placebo (standardized mean difference, - 0.70; 95% confidence interval, - 1.10 to - 0.20), although the certainty of evidence was very low. However, broader clinical translation remains constrained by heterogeneous dosimetry, insufficiently standardized treatment protocols, and uneven evidence maturity across indications. To address these limitations, we propose a precision-oriented framework that links clinical target, tissue-optical context, wavelength selection, patient- and site-specific modifiers, dosimetric implications, measurable endpoints, and evidence maturity. This framework is intended to support treatment planning, parameter reporting, and prospective validation rather than to prescribe currently validated individualized dosing algorithms.
